flashcard_questions.a: Having enough reliable, affordable energy to meet a population's needs.
When a country produces more energy than it consumes and can sell the excess.
When a country consumes more energy than it produces and has to import.

flashcard_questions.q: What share of the world's energy is used by industry?
What proportion of global energy production comes from fossil fuels?
What is a country's energy mix?
flashcard_questions.a: The proportion of its energy generated from each different source.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are much of Africa and central Asia energy insecure?
flashcard_questions.a: They lack both energy resources and the money to import them.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are the UK and USA only medium energy insecure?
flashcard_questions.a: They produce some energy but must import gas and oil to meet demand.

flashcard_questions.q: Which country supplies much of the gas imported by the UK?
Why does population growth raise global energy demand?
flashcard_questions.a: More people means more homes and factories needing power.

flashcard_questions.q: How does geology affect a country's energy supply?
flashcard_questions.a: It decides how easy and how costly an energy source is to reach.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is extracting fossil fuels in the Arctic so expensive?
flashcard_questions.a: The extreme climate makes the work dangerous and difficult.

flashcard_questions.q: What is exploitation of an energy resource?
flashcard_questions.a: Reaching supplies that were previously too difficult or expensive to access.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to energy prices when a resource becomes harder to find?
flashcard_questions.a: Production falls, prices rise and people use less.

notes: 14 cards: 6 term-to-definition (energy security, surplus, deficit, energy mix, exploitation, geology), 3 figure cards (half of energy to industry, 87% fossil fuels, Russian gas), 5 cause-to-consequence (Africa and central Asia, UK and USA, population growth, Arctic climate, scarcity and prices). Lesson is short on named case studies and carries only two figures, so most cards test the supply-and-demand reasoning rather than statistics.
